items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (BTIG chief technical strategist)
items.title: Every mid-term-year Aug-Oct window since 1990 has dropped >7% except one — and that one already fell 9% beforehand
items.idea: Equal-weight S&P 500 is up ~16% YTD at all-time highs with every sector positive, but RSP hasn't seen a pullback bigger than 2.25% since March, sits ~11% above its 200-day moving average, and the NYSE has logged zero 80%-downside-volume days this year versus a historical average of 21. Every mid-term-election-year August-October window since 1990 has produced at least a 7% drawdown except 2006, and 2006 had already absorbed a 9% decline from May-July.
items.angle: This is a volatility-mispricing setup, not a directional call — when a market forgets what a real selloff feels like right as it enters the seasonally worst stretch of the calendar, cheap tail protection is the trade, not a short.
items.tweetA: Every mid-term election year since 1990 has seen a >7% August-October drawdown except one — and that one had already dropped 9% in May-July. This year: +16% YTD equal-weight, zero 80%-down-volume days, RSP hasn't pulled back 2.25% since March. Skew is broken.
items.tweetB: Zero 80%-downside-volume days in 2026 vs an average of 21. That's not calm markets, that's a market that's forgotten what selling looks like right as it walks into the worst seasonal window on the calendar. Cheap tail hedges here are a gift, not a hobby.

items.title: Three FOMC members dissented in favor of a hike at the meeting that held rates — the market barely noticed
items.idea: At the July 28-29 FOMC meeting, the committee held rates at 3.50-3.75%, but three members dissented in favor of a hike, an unusually hawkish internal split for a 'hold' decision. Wednesday's minutes release is the next test of whether that dissent reflected genuine inflation concern or was noise around softer data.
items.angle: A 3-dissent hawkish split inside a headline 'hold' is a bigger tell about the Fed's internal reaction function than the rate decision itself, and it's the kind of detail that gets buried under the seasonality/Hormuz/earnings headlines this week.
items.tweetA: Buried in the July FOMC recap: they held at 3.50-3.75%, but THREE members wanted a hike. That's an unusually hawkish dissent count for a 'hold' and the market barely blinked. Wednesday's minutes are going to matter more than people think.
items.tweetB: The market is pricing a benign Fed. Three dissenting hawks at the last meeting say otherwise. If the minutes show that dissent was about sticky inflation rather than data noise, September odds get repriced fast.

items.title: Florida 2000 wasn't decided by persuasion — it was decided by who controlled the counting machinery and the clock. 2026 is replaying the setup earlier.
items.idea: The 2000 Florida recount (537-vote certified margin, 36 days of litigation, Bush v. Gore citing the federal 'safe harbor' deadline) shows deadlines becoming leverage once an election margin falls inside a system's error band. In August 2026: the DOJ may take its voter-roll dispute with states to the Supreme Court (Aug 16), a federal judge blocked USPS mail-in voting restrictions (Aug 12), and a voting-machine cybersecurity firm faced backlash after finding no fraud (Aug 13) — administrative disputes are migrating into courts before the midterms even arrive.
items.angle: Florida's August 18 primary under new congressional maps is the live stress test — a messy county-level count (late mail ballots, tabulation errors, voter-roll litigation) is the preview of how contested November could get, not the primary result itself.
items.tweetA: 2000 taught us that once an election margin gets thin enough, it isn't decided by persuasion — it's decided by who controls the counting machinery and the clock. 2026 has the same fight starting earlier: DOJ vs. states on voter rolls is headed toward SCOTUS before a single midterm vote is cast.
items.tweetB: Florida's Aug 18 primary is the first test of new congressional maps. A clean count tells you nothing. A messy one — late mail ballots, county delays, tabulation disputes — is the preview of how ugly November could get. Watch it as a systems stress test, not a horse race.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (on Morgan Stanley research)
items.title: Morgan Stanley's own AI model shows falling token prices colliding with infrastructure costs that aren't falling at all
items.idea: Morgan Stanley's generative-AI assumptions show token prices falling while the compute infrastructure to produce them stays enormously expensive — economics that look more like a commodity business carrying software-style capex than a software business. Hyperscalers hold the strongest hand today because they own the compute and collect the rent, but that depends on GPU rental prices staying far more durable than prior hardware cycles.
items.angle: The real bear case was never 'AI fails' — it's 'AI succeeds spectacularly while investors fight over who actually earns an adequate return on the trillions committed to the buildout,' and today that return is concentrated in whoever owns the metal, not the model.
items.tweetA: Morgan Stanley's own numbers say the quiet part: token prices are falling while the infrastructure to make them stays brutally expensive. That's not a software margin profile — that's a commodity business wearing a software valuation.
items.tweetB: The real AI bear case was never 'it doesn't work.' It's 'it works so well that competition crushes pricing while capex stays fixed' — the trillions get spent, the value gets created, and equity holders fight over table scraps. Ask who owns pricing power today: the hyperscalers renting the GPUs, not the model labs.

items.title: SemiAnalysis reverse-engineered PJM's black-box grid model and found it cost 66 million ratepayers $12 billion
items.idea: After 6 months reverse-engineering PJM's opaque Reserve Requirement Study, SemiAnalysis found the model underestimates existing generation capacity by ~4GW because it ignores that gas plants run up to 25% more efficiently in cold winter air and doesn't credit that 400 of PJM's ~700 gas plants invested in winterization after Storm Elliott. Better modeling would have saved $6.7B in 2025/26 (procuring just 14MW less power) and $4.9B in 2026/27 (0.8GW less) — the savings are wildly non-linear because PJM is operating at its supply limit. PJM's upcoming 'emergency auction' (Sept 30-Oct 21) will sign 6.8GW of contracts running to 2043, paid whether or not forecast datacenter demand ever shows up, with zero committed counterparties so far.
items.angle: This is the AI power bill being socialized in real time — if no hyperscaler signs on as counterparty to the emergency auction, residential ratepayers are the default backstop for capacity built to insure against datacenter demand that may never arrive.
items.tweetA: $12B. That's what SemiAnalysis calculates PJM overcharged 66M ratepayers 2025-27 because its capacity model can't account for cold air making gas plants ~25% stronger in winter. $6.7B of that came from procuring just 14MW LESS power — the auction math is that non-linear at the margin.
items.tweetB: PJM's emergency auction signs contracts running to 2043, gets paid whether or not the datacenter demand it's insuring against ever shows up, and currently has zero committed counterparties. If no hyperscaler signs on, residential ratepayers are the backstop by default. The AI buildout's power bill is being socialized in real time.

items.title: Hormuz traffic is down 80-90% and still closed, and the Iran-US MoU expires this week with 'zero progress' in 60 days
items.idea: The Iran-US memorandum of understanding was set to expire the day after this note, with the author noting zero progress in the prior 60 days. The Strait of Hormuz remains closed with traffic collapsed 80-90% since the war began; Trump's claim the US 'owns' the strait carries no operational meaning. Separately, a sitting former Congresswoman (Marjorie Taylor Greene) publicly claimed the White House is discussing nuclear options against Iran in strategy meetings — unverified, but notable that it's plausible enough to circulate.
items.angle: Oil isn't pricing a supply crisis because the market has priced this as a frozen conflict, but a frozen conflict is not the same as a resolved one, and this week's MoU expiry is the first concrete date where that assumption gets tested.
items.tweetA: Hormuz traffic is down 80-90% since the war started and the Strait is STILL closed — yet oil isn't pricing a supply crisis because everyone's assuming this stays frozen. The Iran-US MoU expires this week. 'Frozen conflict' isn't the same as 'resolved.'
items.tweetB: A sitting former Congresswoman just said the White House is discussing nuclear options against Iran in strategy meetings. Verified or not, the fact that this claim is plausible enough to make news shows how far the Overton window on this conflict has already moved.

items.title: Stocks and yields are both rising together in the US and Japan, breaking the textbook inverse relationship in both places at once
items.idea: The 10Y Treasury yield hasn't made a higher high since late 2023 despite three years of 'surging yields' headlines — a range, not a real uptrend, though it keeps grinding toward the author's 4.8% ceiling. Meanwhile equities keep rising alongside those yields, bucking the textbook inverse relationship. The same decoupling shows up in Japan: JGB yields rising, yet the Nikkei 225, the DXJ hedged-equity ETF, and Japanese small caps are all in clean uptrends simultaneously.
items.angle: Seeing the same yields-up-stocks-up decoupling in two different sovereign bond markets at once is a stronger signal than either one alone — it suggests a structural repricing of the yield-equity relationship, not a US-specific anomaly.
items.tweetA: The textbook says rising yields should hurt stocks. Nikkei, DXJ, and Japanese small caps are all near highs while JGB yields climb. The US is doing the same thing. Either the textbook relationship is dead, or everyone's about to relearn why it existed.
items.tweetB: 10Y hasn't made a higher high since late 2023 — three years sideways, not actually a breakout despite the constant headlines about 'surging yields.' The real story isn't the level, it's that equities have stopped caring about the level at all.

items.title: Hartnett names a specific 3-week sequence — Jackson Hole, FOMC, a possible BOJ hike — as the trigger for a yield-peak 'Mission Accomplished' moment
items.idea: Hartnett's chain: a hawkish Warsh speech at Jackson Hole (Aug 28), the September 16 FOMC, and a potential BOJ hike (Sept 18) could together cap long-end yields and deflate the yen-collapse trade. Debt service is near $1.4 trillion; quiet outperformance in REITs, biotech, regional banks and small caps suggests markets are already sniffing a yield peak. Hartnett stays strategically long the AI bubble in equities while shorting AI bonds, arguing capex is exploding while cash flow deteriorates.
items.angle: Long the AI bubble, short AI bonds is the cleanest expression of 'the equity story and the credit story have diverged' — the debt gets repriced before the equity does, and the REIT/small-cap outperformance is the tell that positioning is already rotating ahead of the Sept 16-18 window.
items.tweetA: Hartnett's calling a specific 3-week window — Jackson Hole Aug 28, FOMC Sept 16, possible BOJ hike Sept 18 — as the sequence that caps long yields and kills the yen-collapse trade. If he's right, REITs/regional banks/small caps (already quietly outperforming) front-ran it.
items.tweetB: Long the AI bubble, short AI bonds — that's Hartnett's actual position, and it's the cleanest 'equity story and credit story have diverged' trade I've seen. Capex is exploding, cash flow isn't following, and the debt gets priced before the equity does.

items.tweetA: Kalshi's odds that Hormuz traffic normalizes by year-end have crashed from 86% in June to 34% now. That's the market quietly repricing 'this ends soon' to 'this is the new normal,' and almost nobody's talking about the odds move itself, just the headline event.
items.tweetB: China's July retail sales are forecast to soften to just 0.9% YoY, industrial production to 4.9%. Everyone's obsessing over the Fed's next 25bp. The bigger structural story might be China decelerating into a stimulus vacuum while the US argues about rate cuts.

items.title: Yields rose on a -0.6% retail sales miss, and only 8% of consumers now expect income to outpace inflation, down from 18% in December 2024
items.idea: July retail sales came in at -0.6%, Goldman cut its Q3 GDP estimate by half a point to 2.2% on the print, yet 10Y yields rose anyway. University of Michigan sentiment printed 51.0 versus ~54.5-54.7 expected, with only 8% of consumers now expecting income growth to exceed inflation over the next year, down from 18% in December 2024. July's budget deficit hit $432B, the largest ever recorded for that month, with national debt on track to exceed $40 trillion by Labor Day. A Luke Gromen framework frames the US choice as either 'winning' (negative real rates, a gold-backed reserve reset, bondholders losing in real terms) or 'losing' (higher rates choking growth while China outbuilds the US military).
items.angle: Yields no longer responding to weak growth data the way the textbook says they should is the tell that deficit dynamics ($432B in one month, $40T by Labor Day) have become the dominant driver of the long end, not the business cycle — which is the whole case for gold regardless of which Fed meeting is next.
items.tweetA: Only 8% of US consumers now expect their income to outpace inflation next year, down from 18% in Dec 2024. That collapse in confidence is happening while the stock market sits at highs. Somebody's wrong, and it's usually not the people describing their own paycheck.
items.tweetB: Yields rose on a -0.6% retail sales miss. That's the tell — bond math has stopped responding to weak growth data because the deficit ($432B in July, worst ever for the month, $40T debt by Labor Day) is now the bigger story than the business cycle. Gold doesn't care why real rates go negative, only that they do.

items.title: A historian's framing: governments destroying their own records isn't usually a democracy's move — and ~5,000 USAID reports just vanished
items.idea: Frankopan frames evidence destruction as historically a signature of regimes in transition trying to erase what they did before successors can find out, rare in stable democracies rather than autocracies. Since the Trump administration began dismantling USAID last year, roughly 5,000 of the 25 years of evaluation and audit reports stored in USAID's Development Experience Clearinghouse have been deleted.
items.angle: This isn't really an aid-policy story, it's a data-loss story — every future researcher, auditor, or journalist trying to evaluate US foreign aid effectiveness has just permanently lost a chunk of the primary source base, which is a different kind of damage than a funding cut.
items.tweetA: A historian's framing worth sitting with: destroying government records isn't usually something stable democracies do to themselves — it's what regimes do on their way out, to make it harder for successors to reconstruct what happened. ~5,000 USAID evaluation and audit reports, 25 years of institutional evidence, quietly deleted this year.
items.tweetB: The USAID document purge isn't really an aid story, it's a data story. Every future researcher, auditor, or journalist trying to evaluate US foreign aid effectiveness just lost their primary source base. That's a permanent information loss, not a policy debate.
